doc.title: Bobby Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Starting clarinet with family friend Joe Marsala
summary: Gordon began lessons at eleven or twelve with Joe Marsala, rode the train to New York to meet Pee Wee Russell, Condon and others, and first heard Marsala as a small child in Hartford.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: And how did you get your start in the world of music?

Well when I was eleven or twelve years old I had a very close friend of my family, his name was Joe Marsala, who was a clarinetist in his own right, he had his own band on 52nd Street, and played with Wingy Manone, played with Louis Prima, played with all of — Bobby Hackett, Eddie Condon, played with all the great bands and he kind of took me under his wing and started giving me clarinet lessons. I asked to have them and it was a good experience because I would go out on location to jobs with him when he used to go to play in New York City. He’d take me on the train and we’d ride in and I got a chance to meet Pee Wee Russell and I got a chance to meet Eddie Condon and George Wettling and Muggsy Spanier and all these people.
That’s pretty fascinating for a young man.
Yeah. Well I was about twelve or thirteen years old at the time and it was really something else, really something to see.
Was that the heyday of 52nd Street?
No, 52nd was a little bit before that, but this was after 52nd Street.
And how long did you stay in New York?
Oh, I stayed in New York up until the time I was, around 38 or 39 and then I moved back out to the coast.
When did you think that you were going to be a musician?

Well my dad used to take me down — I’m from Hartford, Connecticut originally, and my dad used to take me down to the State Theatre, which was an old dance place and they showed movies and they had dance bands there. And I saw Joe Marsala play and that brought my interest in the music. I was about four or five years old at the time. And I
used to listen to records, and my dad was in the record business in Hartford and New York, and also in the publishing business, so it was kind of instilled in me and my family, to like music.
So your association with Joe was directly responsible for your picking up the clarinet?
